kurals.tamil:
செருக்குஞ் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்
பெருக்கம் பெருமித நீர்த்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Serukkunj chinamum sirumaiyum illaar
Perukkam perumitha neerththu.
kurals.meaning: The prosperity of those who are free from arrogance, anger, and base desire carries real dignity and is held in honour.
kurals.elementary: Some people get rich and then turn bossy, angry, and greedy for low pleasures. This kural says that when someone does well in life but stays humble, calm, and clean-minded, their success is the kind people truly respect.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by naming three faults (குற்றம்) a ruler must purge: செருக்கு (arrogance, the swelling of self that success breeds), சினம் (anger), and சிறுமை (literally ‘smallness’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss it as காமம், base lust or petty desire). The claim is conditional and political: பெருக்கம் (increase, prosperity) only becomes பெருமிதம் (dignity, honourable greatness) when these three are absent. Wealth and power are morally neutral amplifiers; what they amplify is character. The triadic diagnosis of pride, anger and desire as the roots of ruin is one of the most widely shared moral analyses across ancient traditions, from the Gita’s ‘demoniac’ qualities to the Mishnah’s list of things that ‘put a man out of the world’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bewildered by false ego, strength, pride, lust and anger, the demons become envious of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is situated in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, and blaspheme against the real religion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes how people with power and strength are knocked off balance by ego, pride, lust and anger, and turn against what is good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural name nearly the same cluster of faults (pride, lust, anger) as what corrupts the strong; the Kural states the positive side: strength without them is honourable.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong overlap on the triad of faults; the Gita frames it theologically (envy of God), the Kural politically (dignity of prosperity).

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John names desire and pride as the marks of a worldly life that pulls a person away from God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts single out desire and pride as the faults that spoil a life; the Kural adds anger and applies it to prosperous rulers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Two of the three faults match (lust, pride); anger is absent and the focus is world-renunciation rather than dignified prosperity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises those who stay generous in good and bad times and who hold back their anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: Restraining anger while prospering is exactly what the Kural says makes success dignified.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches only the anger element (plus generosity, which anticipates Kurals 432 and 437); arrogance and lust are not named here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: A rabbi of the Mishnah lists three inner drives that drive a person out of a good life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah diagnoses character through a triad of faults; lust and craving for honour (a form of arrogance) overlap directly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (triad of ruinous faults); envy replaces anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should give up anger, renounce pride, and overcome all fetters. Suffering never befalls him who clings not to mind and body and is detached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches letting go of anger and pride, and cutting the fetters of craving, so that suffering no longer takes hold.
buddhism.tie_back: The same three faults, anger, pride and craving, are named as what must be dropped; the Kural says the reward is dignified prosperity, the Dhammapada says freedom from suffering.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on faults; the goal differs (liberation versus honourable worldly success).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe, queen of Thebes, rich in wealth and fourteen children, boasts that she is greater than the goddess Leto and forbids her worship; Apollo and Artemis kill her children and she is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: A queen with everything turns arrogant about her good fortune, and her pride destroys all she has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The negative image of the Kural: prosperity joined to arrogance loses its dignity and ends in ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates only the arrogance element, by counter-example; anger and lust are not in view.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato divides the soul into reason, spirit (the seat of anger) and appetite (desire), and argues that a person, like a city, is just and well-ordered only when reason governs spirit and appetite.
philosophy.explanation: Plato thinks a good life needs your thinking mind in charge of your temper and your cravings.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s absence of anger and base desire is what Plato calls the rule of reason over spirit and appetite; both link inner order to worthy public standing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual parallel; Plato’s framework is psychological theory rather than a list of faults, and arrogance is not separately treated.

kurals.tamil:
இவறலும் மாண்பிறந்த மானமும் மாணா
உவகையும் ஏதம் இறைக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ivaralum maanbirandha maanamum maanaa
Uvakaiyum yedham iraikku.
kurals.meaning: Avarice, pride that has lost all worth, and unseemly delight are faults that harm a ruler.
kurals.elementary: A leader should not be stingy, should not be proud about the wrong things, and should not enjoy things that are low or harmful. This kural says those three habits are dangers for anyone in charge.
kurals.university: Valluvar adds a second triad specific to kingship (இறை, ‘the ruler’): இவறல் (miserliness, refusing to give what should be given), மாண்பு இறந்த மானம் (a sense of honour that has ‘died to excellence’, i.e. touchy pride over the wrong things; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as refusing to bow to the worthy out of pride of office), and மாணா உவகை (joy in what is unworthy). ஏதம் means harm or fault. Each is a perversion of a legitimate royal trait: prudence with wealth decays into avarice, dignity into vanity, and a king’s pleasures into indulgence. Miserliness returns in Kurals 437 and 438 as the gravest of all faults, so this couplet frames the chapter’s political core: a ruler’s private vices become public dangers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the traits of the ‘demoniac’ character, with pride and conceit at the head.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘pride that has lost all worth’ is the Gita’s pride, arrogance and conceit, marked as a fault of character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the false-pride element only; avarice and unworthy joy are not in this verse, and the Gita is not addressed to rulers specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the qualities a church leader must have: not given to drink, not violent, not greedy for money.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set out the disqualifying faults of a leader, and both put love of money and self-indulgent pleasure among them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on leadership framing, avarice and improper pleasure (wine); false pride is covered only indirectly (1 Tim 3:6 warns against being ‘lifted up with pride’).

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Qārūn was from the people of Moses, but he tyrannized them. And We gave him of treasures whose keys would burden a band of strong men; thereupon his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, Allāh does not like the exultant.”
islam.explanation: Qarun (Korah) was given enormous wealth, grew arrogant and oppressive, and gloated over his riches; his people warned him against this boastful delight.
islam.tie_back: Qarun embodies all three faults of the Kural: hoarded wealth, arrogant pride and unworthy exultation, and his story ends in ruin (28:81).
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on all three faults in one figure; Qarun is a wealthy man of influence rather than a king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s law of the king forbids him to pile up wives and wealth for himself, and (17:20) warns ‘that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren’.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Torah names the specific faults that endanger a ruler: self-serving wealth, indulgence and a heart lifted up in pride.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (rules for the ruler’s character); the Torah targets accumulation rather than miserly refusal to give.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The ‘ten royal virtues’ (dasa-rājadhamma) listed in the Jātaka commentary begin with dāna (generosity) and include maddava (gentleness, freedom from haughtiness), tapa (self-restraint in pleasures) and akkodha (non-anger).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist tradition teaches that a good king must be generous, gentle rather than proud, and restrained in his pleasures.
buddhism.tie_back: Each of the Kural’s three royal faults is the opposite of one of these virtues: avarice versus generosity, false pride versus gentleness, unworthy joy versus restraint.
buddhism.source: Dasa-rājadhamma, Jātaka commentary (e.g. Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, J 534)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic match as the virtue side of the Kural’s vices; paraphrased list, not a verbatim quote, and the exact Jātaka location is given as a commonly cited example.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Croesus of Lydia shows the Athenian sage Solon his treasuries and waits to be called the happiest of men; Solon refuses to call anyone happy before seeing his end, and Croesus later loses his kingdom to Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A rich king delights in his wealth and his own greatness, ignores a wise warning, and falls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus shows the Kural’s danger: a ruler’s pride in wealth and misplaced delight in fortune blind him to ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Legendary history rather than myth; matches pride and unworthy delight, but Croesus is famous for lavish giving, not avarice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato has Socrates decree that the city’s guardians must own no private property and may not touch or possess gold and silver, so that greed does not turn them from guardians into tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: Plato thought rulers should be kept away from private riches because love of money ruins people in power.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Plato and the Kural treat the ruler’s relationship to wealth as a question of character that decides whether rule helps or harms.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Plato’s remedy is structural (no property), while the Kural targets the ruler’s inner vice; pride and unworthy joy are not addressed.

kurals.tamil:
தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் வரினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பழிநாணு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyaang kutram varinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar pazhinaanu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who dread disgrace, even if a fault as small as a millet seed arises in them, will treat it as though it were as large as a palmyra tree.
kurals.elementary: A millet seed is tiny, and a palm tree is huge. People who really care about doing right treat even a tiny mistake as if it were a giant one, so they fix it straight away instead of letting it grow.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a vivid scale contrast between தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains) and பனை (the palmyra palm, among the tallest trees). பழிநாணுவார், ‘those who are ashamed before blame’, are defined not by having no faults but by how they perceive them: they magnify their own errors in their own eyes. This is a moral psychology of vigilance. Shame (நாண்) works here as a protective faculty, the Tamil counterpart of Greek aidōs, that makes a small lapse feel intolerable before it can grow. The commentators divide on whether the sense is ‘they grieve over it as if it were huge’ (Puliyur Kesikan) or ‘they guard against it as if it were huge’ (Varadarasan, Karunanidhi); both readings share the principle of disproportionate self-scrutiny.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that, for someone of honour, a disgraced name is harder to bear than death.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who dread disgrace’ are exactly the people for whom, as the Gita says, dishonour weighs more than death, which is why they treat even small faults as huge.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the fear-of-disgrace motive; the Gita does not make the small-fault-as-large-fault comparison.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that how someone handles very small things reveals how they will handle big ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts refuse to treat small faults as trivial; the millet-sized fault matters because character is built on the least things.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on the significance of small faults; the shame motive is not explicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer sees his sins as if he were sitting under a mountain which, he is afraid, may fall on him; whereas the wicked person considers his sins as flies passing over his nose and he just drives them away like this.”
islam.explanation: Ibn Mas‘ud contrasts the believer, who feels even his sins as a mountain about to fall, with the wicked person, who brushes them off like flies.
islam.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: the conscientious person sees a small fault as a mountain (palmyra) rather than as something tiny (millet, a fly).
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the magnification image; note this portion is Ibn Mas‘ud’s own saying within the narration.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one, for you did know not the reward for the fulfillment of the commandments.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince teaches that small duties deserve as much care as big ones, since we cannot know their true weight.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘treat the small as great’ is the Mishnah’s ‘be as careful with the light as with the grave’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in principle; the Mishnah speaks of commandments to keep rather than faults to avoid.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, 'It will not come to me.' Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that small wrongdoings, repeated, fill a person with evil just as drops of water fill a pot.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say that no fault is small enough to ignore; the wise person, like the Kural’s shame-sensitive person, treats the drop as seriously as the flood.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on refusing to minimise small faults; the Dhammapada argues by accumulation, the Kural by perception and shame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes how, in the degenerate Iron Age, Aidōs (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) will abandon humankind and depart to the gods, leaving no defence against evil.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, Shame is a goddess, and when she leaves the human world, people lose what kept them from wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s பழிநாணுவார் are those in whom Aidōs still lives: their sense of shame is the faculty that makes even small faults feel large.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches the role of shame as a guardian against wrong; there is no small-versus-large fault imagery.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Shame should not be described as a virtue; for it is more like a feeling than a state of character. It is defined, at any rate, as a kind of fear of dishonour...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses shame as a fear of disgrace that restrains people, especially the young, from doing wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who dread disgrace’ are defined by exactly this fear of dishonour, which drives them to magnify their own faults.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Defines the Kural’s motive (fear of disgrace) precisely, but Aristotle does not praise magnifying small faults and treats shame as below full virtue.

kurals.tamil:
குற்றமே காக்க பொருளாகக் குற்றமே
அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kutrame kaakka porulaakak kutrame
Atran tharooum pakai.
kurals.meaning: Make it your chief aim to guard against faults, for it is fault itself that is the enemy that brings ruin.
kurals.elementary: We often worry about enemies outside us. This kural says the most dangerous enemy is a bad habit or mistake inside ourselves, because that is what can truly destroy us. So guarding against our own faults should be our main job.
kurals.university: The repetition of குற்றமே (‘fault itself’) in both lines is emphatic: the ēkāram singles out fault, not external foes, as the true enemy. பொருளாக can be read as ‘as the essential aim’ or, with a pun on பொருள் (wealth, the theme of the whole Porutpāl), ‘as though it were your treasure’: guarding against faults is to be protected like wealth. அற்றம் means ruin or destruction, and தரூஉம் is the prolonged (alapedai) form of தரும், ‘that which brings’. (The two digitised editions consulted print ‘த்ரூஉம்’, a typographical slip for தரூஉம்.) The political reading (Solomon Pappaiah) is that a state is destroyed less by invading armies than by the ruler’s own moral failings, which is the governing thesis of this chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the real enemy is not outside him but the desire and anger within.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural and the Gita both locate the decisive enemy inside the self; the Kural calls it fault, the Gita names lust turning into wrath.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the inner-enemy idea; the Gita names one specific fault rather than fault in general.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
christianity.explanation: God warns Cain that sin is crouching at his door like a predator, and that he must master it.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture wrongdoing as an enemy lying in wait, and both command vigilant guarding against it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong imagery match (fault as hostile predator to be mastered); shared by Jewish and Christian readers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Joseph, the speaker admits that his own soul constantly urges him toward evil, and only God’s mercy protects him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s enemy within is the Quran’s nafs that ‘persistently enjoins evil’; both demand watchfulness over oneself.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the inner source of fault; the Quran stresses reliance on divine mercy, the Kural on self-guarding.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So too the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created an evil inclination, which is the wound, and I created Torah as its antidote.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud describes the evil inclination as a wound inside each person, and Torah study as the bandage that keeps it from festering; it cites Genesis 4:7, ‘Sin crouches at the door’.
judaism.tie_back: The yetzer hara is the Kural’s inner enemy, and the constant remedy of Torah is the constant guarding the Kural commands.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the inner enemy and the need for ongoing protection; the Talmud’s remedy is specifically Torah study.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that no external enemy can hurt you as badly as your own badly directed mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s claim: one’s own fault is a worse enemy than any outside foe.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel; the Kural adds the practical command to make guarding one’s chief aim.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon, reconciling with Achilles, says his ruinous insult was the work of Atē, the goddess of blind folly, who walks on men’s heads and brings them to harm.
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon admits a fault of his own nearly destroyed the Greek army, and describes it as a goddess of ruin that seized him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Iliad personifies fault as a destroying power, as the Kural calls fault an enemy that brings ruin; Agamemnon’s near-defeat came from his own error, not from Troy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Agamemnon partly shifts blame onto Atē, which is almost the opposite of the Kural’s call for self-responsibility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...know this of a truth - that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: Facing execution, Socrates insists that nothing outside can truly harm a good person.
philosophy.tie_back: If no outside evil can ruin the good, then, as the Kural says, the only real enemy is one’s own fault.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Implicit parallel only; Socrates states the corollary (outside harm is powerless) rather than naming fault as the enemy.

kurals.tamil:
வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் வாழ்க்கை எரிமுன்னர்
வைத்தூறு போலக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Varumunnark kaavaathaan vaazhkkai erimunnar
Vaiththooru polak kedum.
kurals.meaning: The life of one who does not guard against faults before they arrive will perish like a heap of straw placed before a fire.
kurals.elementary: Dry straw near a fire catches in a flash. This kural says that if you don’t protect yourself from mistakes before they happen, your life can go up in flames just as quickly.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallel of two முன்னர் (‘before’): வருமுன்னர் (before [the fault] comes) and எரிமுன்னர் (before the fire). Failure to act in the first ‘before’ puts one in the second. வைத்தூறு is a stack of straw (வைக்கோல் போர்), the most combustible of village materials, so the image stresses how sudden and total the ruin is once prevention has failed. This is the chapter’s case for preventive rather than corrective vigilance: once a fault has taken hold, correction may already be too late. The same principle appears in Valluvar’s wider political thought on foresight (compare Kural 442 in the next chapter, which praises counsellors who guard against troubles before they arrive).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, Anāgatavidhātā (‘Forethought’) leaves the pond as soon as he hears fishermen plan to return, Pratyutpannamati (‘Ready-wit’) escapes by a trick, and Yadbhaviṣya (‘Whatever-will-be’) waits and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: Three fish hear danger coming; only the one who acts before it arrives is fully safe, and the one who waits is destroyed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘guard before it comes’ is the lesson of Anāgatavidhātā; the fish who waits is the straw before the fire.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (fable of the three fish)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on foresight versus delay; the danger in the fable is external rather than a personal fault.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the prudent, who see trouble coming and take cover, with the simple, who walk on into it.
christianity.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: guarding in advance saves you, carelessness leads to ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel on foresight; the Kural’s fire-and-straw image stresses the speed of ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allāh. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow - and fear Allāh. Indeed, Allāh is Aware of what you do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran urges each person to look ahead and consider what their deeds are preparing for the future.
islam.tie_back: Both call for looking ahead at the consequences of one’s conduct before it is too late; this verse is a classic basis for muhāsaba (self-accounting).
islam._accuracy_note: Matches forethought and self-examination; the ‘tomorrow’ here is primarily the Hereafter rather than worldly ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is the wise person? The one who sees and anticipates the consequences of his behavior.”
judaism.explanation: The sages, answering Alexander the Great, define wisdom as foreseeing where one’s actions will lead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who ‘guards before it comes’ is the Talmud’s wise one who sees what is coming from his conduct.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on foresight regarding one’s own conduct; no image of sudden ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells monks to guard themselves like a frontier town, because those who waste their chance come to grief.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts call for guarding oneself before the danger strikes, and both warn of irreversible ruin for those who neglect it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on constant pre-emptive guarding; the ruin envisaged is rebirth in hell rather than a worldly collapse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And Epimetheus did not think on what Prometheus had said to him, bidding him never take a gift of Olympian Zeus... But he took the gift, and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) ignores his brother Prometheus (‘Forethought’), accepts Pandora, and understands the danger only after the evils are loose.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Epimetheus is the Kural’s man who does not guard ‘before it comes’; understanding after the fact cannot put the fire out.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent match on foresight versus hindsight; the harm is cosmic rather than a personal fault.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best plan is to reject straightway the first incentives to anger, to resist its very beginnings, and to take care not to be betrayed into it: for if once it begins to carry us away, it is hard to get back again into a healthy condition...”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that a passion must be stopped at its first stirring, because once it takes over, reason can no longer control it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural and Seneca share the logic of prevention: stop the fault before it enters, because once it catches, like fire in straw, it is too late.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) I.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on pre-emptive guarding; Seneca discusses anger specifically, the Kural faults in general.

kurals.tamil:
தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
என்குற்ற மாகும் இறைக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thankutram neekkip pirarkutrang kaankirpin
Enkutra maakum iraikku.
kurals.meaning: If a ruler first removes his own faults and only then examines the faults of others, what fault could ever befall him?
kurals.elementary: It is easy to spot what others are doing wrong. This kural says a good leader first looks at and fixes their own mistakes, and only then points out other people’s. A leader who does that has nothing to be blamed for.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s central statement of self-scrutiny and its logic is sequential: தன்குற்றம் நீக்கி (having removed one’s own fault) comes before பிறர்குற்றம் காண் (seeing others’ faults). The verb காண்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to see’) implies that judging others rightly is a capacity earned by self-correction. The closing rhetorical question, என்குற்றம் ஆகும் இறைக்கு (‘what fault would there be for the king?’), expects the answer ‘none’. For a ruler whose office is to judge, this is the ethics of legitimate authority: the right to correct others rests on having corrected oneself. The couplet is the Tamil counterpart of the ‘mote and beam’ teaching and of the fable of the two wallets, but it is framed positively as a programme for governance rather than as a rebuke to hypocrisy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thou seest, O king, the fault of others, even though they be as small as a mustard seed. But seeing, thou noticest not thy own faults even though they be as large as the Vilwa fruit.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala rebukes King Dushyanta, who denies her, for spotting others’ tiny faults while missing his own huge ones.
hinduism.tie_back: Addressed, like the Kural, to a king; it condemns exactly what the Kural says a king must avoid: judging others before seeing one’s own faults.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section LXXIV (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the royal addressee and the small/large contrast (compare also Kural 433).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to remove the plank in their own eye before trying to remove the speck in someone else’s.
christianity.tie_back: Identical order of operations: first remove your own fault, then you can rightly see and correct others’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel; the Kural applies it specifically to a ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of you looks at the mote in his brother's eye while forgetting the stump in his own eye.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayra warns against people who notice a speck in a brother’s eye but forget the log in their own.
islam.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: self-correction must precede correcting others. Elsewhere the Prophet calls the believer ‘the believer’s mirror’ (Abu Dawud 4918), mutual correction resting on sincerity.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match; this is a saying of the Companion Abu Hurayra, not attributed to the Prophet in this narration.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...Reish Lakish says concerning this: Adorn [keshot] yourself and afterward adorn others.”
judaism.explanation: Reish Lakish teaches that you must correct your own conduct before requiring others to correct theirs; the Talmud applies it to a rabbi who first cut down his own trees before ruling that others must cut theirs.
judaism.tie_back: Same order as the Kural, and like the Kural it is applied to a person with authority to judge others.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 107b (also Bava Batra 60b)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on sequence and on the legitimacy of the judge.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that we broadcast others’ faults like chaff in the wind but hide our own, and (Dhp 253) that the fault-finder’s own defilements grow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada describes the problem the Kural solves: because one’s own faults are hard to see, they must be looked for and removed first.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; Dhp 50 (‘let one see one’s own acts, done and undone’) gives the positive instruction.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Jupiter has loaded us with a couple of Wallets: the one, filled with our own vices, he has placed at our backs, {the other}, heavy with those of others, he has hung before. From this circumstance, we are not able to see our own faults: but as soon as others make a slip, we are ready to censure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable says Jupiter hung two bags on every person: others’ faults in front, where we always see them, and our own behind, where we never do.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Explains why the Kural must command the reversal: you have to turn the bag round and deal with your own faults before looking at others’.
greek_mythology.source: Phaedrus, Fables IV.10 (tr. H. T. Riley; Aesopic, Perry 266)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close; a fable of the Aesopic tradition in Latin verse rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The spirit ought to be brought up for examination daily. It was the custom of Sextius when the day was over... to inquire of his spirit: "What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?"”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca describes reviewing his whole day every night, judging himself and correcting his own faults before sleep.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s nightly tribunal is a practical method for the Kural’s first step: finding and removing one’s own faults.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) III.36 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on self-examination; Seneca does not state the second step (then judging others).

kurals.tamil:
செயற்பால செய்யா திவறியான் செல்வம்
உயற்பால தன்றிக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyarpaala seyyaa thivariyaan selvam
Uyarpaala thandrik kedum.
kurals.meaning: The wealth of the miser who does not do what ought to be done with it will not endure; it will perish without being of use.
kurals.elementary: Money is meant to be used for good things: helping people, caring for family, doing what is right. This kural says that if someone just sits on their money out of stinginess, it ends up wasted and lost anyway.
kurals.university: செயற்பால (‘things that ought to be done’) are the proper uses of wealth, which Valluvar elsewhere lists as giving, enjoyment and public works; இவறியான் is the one who clings (from இவறு, to hoard or be miserly). உயற்பாலது அன்றி means ‘without the quality of surviving / being saved’: hoarded wealth has no future. The argument is not only moral but practical: wealth that is not put to use is exposed to theft, confiscation and decay, and so the miser loses both the good he could have done and the wealth itself. The couplet returns to இவறல் from Kural 432 and prepares for 438’s verdict that miserliness is the worst of all faults.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartṛhari teaches that wealth has only three possible fates: giving (dāna), enjoyment (bhoga) and destruction (nāśa); the one who neither gives nor enjoys is left with the third.
hinduism.explanation: A classical Sanskrit verse says money that is not given away or used will simply be destroyed.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s argument: wealth not used for its proper ends ‘perishes without being saved’.
hinduism.source: Bhartṛhari, Nītiśataka (verse on the three fates of wealth, c. 43 in common editions)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in logic; paraphrased because the exact English translation used was not verified, and verse numbering varies by edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten. Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.”
christianity.explanation: James warns the hoarding rich that their piled-up wealth is rotting, and that its decay will testify against them.
christianity.tie_back: Both say hoarded wealth decays uselessly and turns against its owner.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on hoarded wealth perishing; James adds divine judgement.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who hoard gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allāh - give them tidings of a painful punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Quran condemns those who pile up gold and silver without spending it for good.
islam.tie_back: Both condemn hoarding in place of using wealth for its proper purposes.
islam.source: Quran 9:34 (Sahih International, latter part of verse)
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the fault; the consequence is punishment in the Hereafter rather than the wealth itself perishing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) describes wealth hoarded to its owner’s harm and then lost in a bad venture, leaving nothing even for his child.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: wealth kept back instead of used ‘perishes’ without benefit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel on kept wealth perishing uselessly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When his wealth isn't properly put to use, kings make off with it, or thieves make off with it, or fire burns it, or water sweeps it away, or hateful heirs make off with it. Thus his wealth, not properly put to use, goes to waste and not to any good use.”
buddhism.explanation: After a miserly millionaire dies childless and his fortune goes to the king’s treasury, the Buddha explains that unused wealth is like a pure pond no one drinks from.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s ‘not properly put to use, goes to waste’ is the Kural’s ‘perishes without being saved’.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the fate of a miser’s wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that all he touches turn to gold; his food and drink become gold, and he nearly starves amid riches until he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets endless gold but cannot use it for anything, not even to eat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas pictures the Kural’s point that wealth not usable for life’s proper ends is worthless and ruinous.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates useless wealth and greed; Midas is greedy rather than stingy, and his wealth is not lost.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life of money-making is one undertaken under compulsion, and wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that wealth has no value in itself; it is only worth what it is used for.
philosophy.tie_back: If wealth is only ‘useful for something else’, then the miser who never uses it, as the Kural says, has wealth that comes to nothing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.5 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Provides the principle behind the Kural rather than a direct condemnation of hoarding.

kurals.tamil:
பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை எற்றுள்ளும்
எண்ணப் படுவதொன் றன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Patrullam ennum ivaranmai etrullum
Ennap paduvathon randru.
kurals.meaning: The miserliness called a grasping heart is not to be counted among other faults at all; it stands apart as a fault beyond them all.
kurals.elementary: This kural says that stinginess, a heart that grabs and won’t let go, is not just one bad habit on a list. It is in a class of its own, worse than all the others.
kurals.university: பற்றுள்ளம் (‘a clinging heart’) defines இவறன்மை (miserliness) as a disposition of attachment, not merely an act of not giving. The phrase எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்று அன்று (‘it is not a thing to be counted among any [faults]’) is deliberately ambiguous: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘a separate fault that cannot be counted along with others’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it as ‘the most terrible of all faults’. Either way it is the chapter’s climax on avarice, which has now appeared three times (432, 437, 438). The ruler-centred reading matters: a stingy king starves the gifts, rewards and public works on which loyalty and prosperity depend, so his avarice spreads into every other failure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed as one of the three gateways to hell that must be abandoned.
hinduism.tie_back: Both rank greed among the most destructive faults; the Kural goes further and sets it above all others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Greed (lobha) is ranked among the worst, but alongside lust and anger rather than above them; greed is broader than miserliness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls the love of money the root from which all kinds of evil grow.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul sets the grasping attachment to wealth apart from, and beneath, other evils.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on ranking love of money as uniquely grave; Paul frames it as root cause rather than as a category apart.

islam.quote_or_event: “...be on your guard against stinginess for stinginess destroyed those who were before you, as it incited them to shed blood and make lawful what was unlawful for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that stinginess (shuḥḥ) destroyed earlier peoples by driving them to bloodshed and lawbreaking.
islam.tie_back: Both treat miserliness not as a small failing but as a master-fault that leads to every other wrong.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: stinginess singled out as uniquely destructive; compare Quran 59:9 on being ‘protected from the stinginess of his soul’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of character in human beings: One that says: ‘mine is mine, and yours is yours’: this is a commonplace type; and some say this is a sodom-type of character.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah notes that some sages see the attitude ‘what’s mine is mine’ as the character of Sodom, whose sin (Ezekiel 16:49) was not helping the poor.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the refusal to share as worse than it looks: the Kural sets it apart from all faults, the Mishnah links it to Sodom.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the gravity of withholding; the Mishnah records a dispute over whether it is ‘commonplace’ or Sodom-like.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says misers cannot reach heaven, while the wise find joy in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Both single out miserliness as a fault with uniquely serious results.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Condemns miserliness strongly but does not rank it above all other faults.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Demeter’s sacred oak for his own use; she curses him with insatiable hunger, so he consumes all his wealth, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man who grabs for himself is cursed with a craving that can never be satisfied and destroys him completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon dramatises the Kural’s ‘grasping heart’ as a fault that swallows everything else.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates insatiable greed and sacrilege rather than stinginess as such; weak but best available myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But meanness is both incurable (for old age and every disability is thought to make men mean) and more innate in men than prodigality... for not only is it a greater evil than prodigality, but men err more often in this direction...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says stinginess is worse than wastefulness: it is incurable, more natural to people, and more common.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, gives miserliness a special rank as the worse and more stubborn fault.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close; Aristotle compares meanness with its opposite vice rather than with all faults.

kurals.tamil:
வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை நயவற்க
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Viyavarka enjnaandrum thannai nayavarka
Nandri payavaa vinai.
kurals.meaning: Never, at any time, admire yourself; and never desire deeds that bring no good.
kurals.elementary: Being impressed with yourself makes you stop noticing your mistakes. This kural gives two simple rules: never be too proud of yourself, and don’t want to do things that don’t do any good.
kurals.university: Two prohibitions run in parallel: வியவற்க (do not wonder at, marvel at) with தன்னை (oneself), and நயவற்க (do not desire) with நன்றி பயவா வினை (deeds that yield no good). எஞ்ஞான்றும் (‘at any time’) makes the first absolute: even at the height of success, self-admiration is forbidden. The two are causally linked. Self-admiration blinds a person to their own faults, which undoes the self-scrutiny of Kural 436, and a self-admiring ruler is the one most easily drawn into vain, unprofitable projects. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second clause politically: a ruler should not want to do what does not benefit the country and its governance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master...”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists humility and freedom from pride first among the qualities that make up true knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘never admire yourself’ is the Gita’s humility and pridelessness, placed at the head of the virtues.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the first clause (no self-admiration); the second clause on unprofitable deeds is not addressed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that praise should come from others, never from yourself.
christianity.tie_back: Same prohibition as the Kural: never admire or praise yourself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the first clause; says nothing on unprofitable deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not claim yourselves to be pure; He is most knowing of who fears Him.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids people to declare themselves pure or righteous, since only God truly knows who is God-fearing.
islam.tie_back: Both forbid self-admiration; the Quran grounds it in the fact that only God sees the heart.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the first clause.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself, because for such a purpose were you created.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai teaches that even great learning is no reason to admire yourself; you have only done what you were made for.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘never, at any time’, it forbids self-admiration even when there is real achievement.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the first clause; Avot 4:4 (‘be exceeding humble of spirit’) reinforces it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “'Let both laymen and monks think that it was done by me. In every work, great and small, let them follow me' — such is the ambition of the fool; thus his desire and pride increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the fool who wants credit and admiration for everything, so his pride and desire keep growing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn that self-admiration feeds itself and spoils one’s aims; the fool’s wish for credit is the opposite of the Kural’s counsel.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on self-admiration and vain ambition; framed as description of the fool rather than as a command.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus, who has scorned all who love him, falls in love with his own reflection in a pool and wastes away gazing at it, unable to turn from himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: A young man who admires only himself is destroyed by that self-admiration.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Narcissus is the extreme image of the Kural’s first warning: self-admiration leads to deeds that yield nothing and finally to ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of the first clause; his fruitless longing loosely matches the second.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The marks of a proficient are, that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one, says nothing concerning himself as being anybody, or knowing anything: when he is, in any instance, hindered or restrained, he accuses himself...”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says a person making real progress never talks about himself as important, and looks for fault in himself first.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus joins the Kural’s ban on self-admiration with the chapter’s central idea of self-accusation (Kural 436).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the first clause and on self-scrutiny; the second clause is not addressed.

kurals.tamil:
காதல காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்
ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaadhala kaadhal ariyaamai uykkirpin
Edhila edhilaar nool.
kurals.meaning: If one can enjoy what one loves without others knowing one’s desires, the schemes of one’s enemies will come to nothing.
kurals.elementary: If everyone knows exactly what you want most, people who wish you harm can use that to trick you. This kural says a wise leader keeps their wishes private, so enemies have nothing to use against them.
kurals.university: The couplet uses doubled words for effect: காதல காதல் (‘the things one loves, [and] one’s love’) and ஏதில ஏதிலார் (‘come to nothing, [the plans of] strangers/enemies’). ஏதிலார் means those unrelated or hostile, and நூல் here means their ‘science’ or stratagems, the craft by which they plot. உய்க்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to experience/carry out’) makes the condition discretion, not renunciation: the ruler may pursue his desires, but must not let them be known. The logic ties the chapter together. A known weakness or appetite is itself a fault (குற்றம்) in the strategic sense, a gap in the armour. By closing the chapter this way, Valluvar moves from moral self-correction to political self-guarding: the ruler must hide from enemies the very desires that could be used to exploit him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya instructs that the king’s deliberations must be held in secret and guarded so that no outsider learns his plans; others should come to know of an undertaking only once it has begun or been completed.
hinduism.explanation: The ancient Indian manual of statecraft teaches that a king must keep his intentions secret so enemies cannot counter them.
hinduism.tie_back: Same political logic as the Kural: hidden intentions defeat enemies’ schemes.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I, ch. 15 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Close on secrecy defeating enemies; Kautilya speaks of counsel and plans, the Kural of personal desires.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the fool who says everything he thinks with the wise person who holds back.
christianity.tie_back: Both praise keeping one’s inner mind to oneself as a mark of wisdom.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches discretion; the Kural’s specific point about enemies exploiting known desires is absent (the Hebrew may refer to anger held back).

islam.quote_or_event: A widely cited hadith (al-Tabarani) says: seek help in accomplishing your needs through keeping them concealed, for everyone who has a blessing is envied.
islam.explanation: The hadith advises keeping your plans and needs private because others may envy and work against them.
islam.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: concealing one’s desires protects them from those who would spoil them.
islam.source: Al-Tabarani, al-Mu‘jam al-Kabir (hadith on concealment of needs)
islam._accuracy_note: Thematically very close, but paraphrased and flagged: its chain is graded differently by hadith scholars (accepted by some later scholars, weakened by others).

judaism.quote_or_event: “That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.”
judaism.explanation: Samson finally tells Delilah the secret of his strength, and the Philistines use it to capture him.
judaism.tie_back: A negative example of the Kural: once his enemies know what he holds dearest, their scheme succeeds.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative illustration by counter-example; the secret is his vow and strength rather than a desire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise draws its four legs and neck into its shell when a jackal approaches; the jackal waits for any limb to come out, finds no opening, and leaves. The Buddha tells monks to guard their senses the same way so that Māra finds no opening.
buddhism.explanation: By keeping everything tucked away, the tortoise gives its enemy nothing to seize.
buddhism.tie_back: Same strategy as the Kural: by keeping desires hidden and guarded, one gives the enemy no handle, and their schemes fail.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the ‘no opening for the enemy’ logic; the Buddhist enemy is Māra and the aim is restraint, not concealment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus escapes the Cyclops Polyphemus by calling himself ‘Nobody’; but as he sails away he boasts his real name, and Polyphemus uses it to call down Poseidon’s curse on him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hiding his identity saved Odysseus; revealing it gave his enemy what he needed to strike back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both sides of the Kural in one story: concealment defeats the enemy, and self-revelation lets the enemy’s plan succeed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of strategic concealment; he hides his name, not his desires.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon distinguishes secrecy, dissimulation and simulation, praising secrecy as a virtue that protects a person’s affairs, and advising openness in reputation but secrecy in habit.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon argues that a wise person keeps their inner intentions private, because revealing them exposes them to others.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon’s ‘secrecy in habit’ is the Kural’s enjoying one’s desires without others knowing them.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good on the value of secrecy; Bacon is early-modern and speaks of general discretion rather than royal desires and enemies.
